title: When was Beowulf composed?
short: Proposed dates for the poem range from about 700 to the early eleventh century, the date of its only manuscript, and rest on metre, language, palaeography and historical context.

needs.ask: Annotate Old English poems and dated prose for metrical, morphological and orthographic features, marking which are authorial and which scribal, using the Dictionary of Old English Corpus.
Train a dating model only on independently dated Old English texts, treat copying as explicit noise, and test it on held-out texts preserved in late copies.

matters: An early date (before about 750) makes Beowulf a witness to the culture of Christian Mercia or Northumbria and to oral-traditional material close to the migration period; a date in the Viking age or the reign of Cnut makes it a product of Anglo-Scandinavian politics and late West Saxon literary culture. The choice shapes readings of the poem's attitude to pagan ancestors, Danish kings and Christianity, and its use as evidence for early English legend, Germanic heroic tradition and the history of Old English verse.
stuck: The poem survives in one manuscript copied around 1000, so internal evidence of composition date must be separated from changes introduced by copying. Metrical tests such as Kaluza's law depend on phonological distinctions whose dating and dialect distribution are themselves inferred, and the corpus of securely dated Old English verse is very small. Arguments from palaeographic error patterns, vocabulary and historical allusion each point to a range rather than a date, and scholars weigh them differently.
solved: A dating model trained on Old English texts with independently established dates and transmission histories that assigns Beowulf a composition interval with calibrated uncertainty, and that correctly recovers the known dates of held-out texts, including texts preserved only in late copies.
approach: The debate is well mapped by human scholarship: the conference volume Chase (1981), the late-date case of Kiernan (1981), the metrical history of Fulk (1992), Lapidge (2000) on letter-form errors in the archetype, the retrospect of Frank (2007), and the essays in Neidorf (2014). Neidorf (2017) argues that scribal modernization can be separated from the poet's own language.

Teams could build a feature set for every Old English poem and dated prose text from the Dictionary of Old English Corpus and manuscript facsimiles: metrical features such as Kaluza's law, contraction and parasite vowels, along with morphology, vocabulary, spelling layers and scribal error types. Which features count as authorial and which as scribal is the decision that shapes everything downstream, and it belongs with philologists.

The quantitative profiling of Neidorf (2019) shows the method can work at scale; a next step would calibrate a model only on texts with independent dating and treat copying as an explicit source of noise, so that it reports which features drive any estimate.

The rival positions, composition around 700 or earlier versus a tenth- or eleventh-century poem close to the manuscript, make different predictions: an early poem should show archaic metrical patterns that scribes failed to update, while a late one should show them only as imitation. Testing those features against Klaeber's edition, Fulk (2008), and the readings in Electronic Beowulf would show which pattern holds.

A shareable annotated corpus of metrical and orthographic features would be useful for other Old English poems even if Beowulf's date stays contested, and the estimate itself will remain a range of decades or centuries rather than a year.

All key witnesses are already digitized, so the main need is careful philological annotation by Old English specialists, along with continued open access to the Dictionary of Old English Corpus and British Library images.

existing.title: The Dating of Beowulf
existing.note: Conference volume that broke the consensus for an eighth-century date, with several contributors arguing for a Viking-age or later context.

existing.title: Beowulf and the Beowulf Manuscript
existing.venue: New Brunswick: Rutgers University Press; revised edition Ann Arbor: University of Michigan Press, 1996
existing.note: Argued from codicology that the poem was composed or substantially reworked in the early eleventh century, contemporary with the surviving manuscript.

existing.title: A History of Old English Meter
existing.note: Argued that the poem's observance of Kaluza's law and other metrical features requires composition before about 725 if Mercian or about 825 if Northumbrian.

existing.title: Electronic Beowulf
existing.venue: London: British Library; 5th edition, University of Kentucky, 2026
existing.note: Digital edition with high-resolution and ultraviolet images of the manuscript, backlit restorations and images of the early transcripts.

existing.title: The archetype of Beowulf
existing.note: Argued from patterns of scribal letter confusion that the poem descends from an exemplar written in a script used before about 750.

existing.title: A Scandal in Toronto: The Dating of 'Beowulf' a Quarter Century On
existing.note: Retrospective by a contributor to the 1981 volume, reviewing how the debate had developed and questioning the confidence of metrical arguments for an early date.

existing.authors: R. D. Fulk, Robert E. Bjork and John D. Niles, eds.
existing.title: Klaeber's Beowulf, fourth edition
existing.note: Standard critical edition, whose introduction surveys the linguistic and metrical dating evidence and inclines to an early date.

existing.title: The Dating of Beowulf: A Reassessment
existing.note: Essays assembling metrical, lexical, onomastic and palaeographic arguments for composition before about 750.

existing.title: The Transmission of Beowulf: Language, Culture, and Scribal Behavior
existing.note: Separates scribal modernization and error from the poet's archaic language and argues for composition around 700.

existing.authors: Leonard Neidorf, Madison S. Krieger, Michelle Yakubek, Pramit Chaudhuri and Joseph P. Dexter
existing.title: Large-scale quantitative profiling of the Old English verse tradition
existing.note: Stylometric profiling of Old English verse that supports single authorship of Beowulf; it addresses unity rather than date but supplies a computational framework applicable to dating.

archives.collection: Cotton MS Vitellius A XV (Nowell Codex, ff. 94–209, containing Beowulf and Judith)
archives.note: The unique manuscript, fire-damaged in 1731; fully imaged, though British Library online services were disrupted after the 2023 cyberattack.

holdings.name: Cotton MS Vitellius A XV (Southwick and Nowell codices)
holdings.note: The Nowell Codex (ff. 94-209) is the only manuscript of Beowulf, copied around the year 1000; the catalogue record gives its description and fire damage.

holdings.name: Cotton MS Vitellius A XV, digitised volume (Internet Archive)
holdings.note: Page images of the manuscript volume for checking readings against the printed editions.

archives.repository: University of Kentucky and British Library
archives.note: Manuscript images under ordinary, ultraviolet and backlit conditions with textual, grammatical and metrical apparatus.

holdings.name: Electronic Beowulf: The Thorkelin Transcripts
holdings.note: Images of both Thorkelin transcripts, the scribe's copy and Thorkelin's own, made before further losses at the fire-damaged edges.

archives.collection: Thorkelin transcripts A and B of Beowulf (1787–89)
archives.note: Transcripts made before further fire-edge losses, which preserve readings now missing from the manuscript; images are included in Electronic Beowulf.

holdings.name: Thorkelin transcripts of Beowulf
holdings.note: Two late-1780s transcripts of the poem, the first by a copyist and the second by Thorkelin; they preserve some readings now lost from the manuscript.

archives.repository: Dictionary of Old English, University of Toronto
archives.collection: Dictionary of Old English Web Corpus and Dictionary A–I
archives.note: At least one copy of every surviving Old English text, about three million words; corpus access is by subscription.

archives.repository: Old English Poetry in Facsimile project
archives.collection: Linked editions and manuscript images of Old English poems
archives.note: Open-access editions keyed to manuscript images, useful for comparing Beowulf's spelling and metre with poems in the Exeter, Vercelli and Junius manuscripts.
The largest Old English poetic anthology, copied in the later tenth century; the principal comparison corpus for metrical and lexical dating.

holdings.name: The Exeter Book
holdings.note: Complete high-resolution digital copy of the 123 leaves of the principal Old English verse anthology, the main comparison text for metre and vocabulary.
